"What's within 300 meters of this store?" and "what falls within 50
meters of this road?" are the same question underneath: draw a zone
at a fixed distance around a feature, then check what's inside it,
a buffer. The distance is fixed, but what comes out depends entirely
on what went in.

Just want to buffer a file with an adjustable distance, rings, and a
download button, without the rest of the reading? Use the
[standalone tool](/tools/buffer-proximity.html) — same engine, less
prose.

## 1. Why the coordinate system matters here

A buffer distance is a real distance: meters, not degrees of
longitude/latitude, where the same number of degrees covers very
different real distances depending on where on Earth you are. Both
languages below pick a working UTM zone from the data's own
bounding-box center and reproject into it first, same reasoning,
same formula, as this site's [Viewshed](raster-viewshed.qmd) and
[Spatial Clustering](spatial-clustering.qmd) tools: a reasonable
default for one local dataset, not a universally correct choice for
data spanning multiple UTM zones or very large areas.

## 2. Upload your data

::: {#lab-upload}
:::

No file uploaded? Both cells below fall back to the same three fixed
features: a point (a shop), a line (a road segment), and a polygon (a
building footprint), deliberately different geometry types, chosen
to show all three buffer shapes in section 4 with one run. Upload
your own point, line, or polygon file to see the same computation on
real data instead.

## Python

```{.webgeods-python #buffer-proximity-py}
#| package: geopandas
import geopandas as gpd
import numpy as np
from shapely.geometry import Point, LineString, Polygon

# Same three-feature layout as the article's original fixed example --
# used only when nothing was uploaded, chosen specifically to show all
# three buffer shapes (point/line/polygon) in one run.
FALLBACK_NAMES = ["shop", "road segment", "building"]
FALLBACK_GEOMETRIES = [
    Point(12.4700, 41.9000),
    LineString([(12.4720, 41.9010), (12.4740, 41.9005)]),
    Polygon([(12.4678, 41.8988), (12.4682, 41.8988), (12.4682, 41.8992), (12.4678, 41.8992)])
]

gdf = None
for path in ["/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip"]:
    try:
        gdf = gpd.read_file(path)
        break
    except Exception:
        pass

crs_warning = None
if gdf is None:
    gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"name": FALLBACK_NAMES}, geometry=FALLBACK_GEOMETRIES, crs="EPSG:4326")
else:
    if gdf.crs is None:
        gdf = gdf.set_crs("EPSG:4326")
        crs_warning = "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
    elif str(gdf.crs) != "EPSG:4326":
        gdf = gdf.to_crs("EPSG:4326")
    if "name" not in gdf.columns:
        gdf["name"] = [f"feature {i + 1}" for i in range(len(gdf))]

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- see section 1 above.
minx, miny, maxx, maxy = gdf.total_bounds
center_lon = float((minx + maxx) / 2)
center_lat = float((miny + maxy) / 2)
utm_zone = int((center_lon + 180) // 6) + 1
calc_epsg = 32600 + utm_zone if center_lat >= 0 else 32700 + utm_zone

gdf_proj = gdf.to_crs(epsg=calc_epsg)

# A single UTM zone can map far-away features to infinity. Shapely
# tolerates it without crashing (an inf-coordinate buffer() just comes
# back empty), but an empty buffer is still a feature that silently
# produced nothing -- excluded here instead, with a clear count.
finite_mask = gdf_proj.geometry.bounds.apply(
    lambda row: all(np.isfinite(v) for v in row), axis=1
)
excluded_count = int((~finite_mask).sum())
gdf_proj = gdf_proj[finite_mask]
gdf_kept = gdf[finite_mask.values]
if len(gdf_proj) == 0:
    raise ValueError(
        f"None of the {len(gdf)} features could be projected into a single "
        f"UTM zone (EPSG:{calc_epsg}) -- this dataset spans too wide an "
        "area for this article's single-zone approach. Try a smaller, more "
        "local file."
    )

buffered_proj = gdf_proj.buffer(30)

buffered_wgs84 = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"name": gdf_kept["name"].values}, geometry=buffered_proj, crs=calc_epsg).to_crs("EPSG:4326")

{
    "features": buffered_wgs84.__geo_interface__,
    "originalFeatures": gdf.__geo_interface__,
    "calculationCrs": f"EPSG:{calc_epsg}",
    "geometryTypes": list(gdf.geometry.geom_type),
    "bufferGeometryTypes": list(buffered_proj.geom_type),
    "bufferAreas": [round(a, 1) for a in buffered_proj.area],
    "excludedCount": excluded_count,
    "crsWarning": crs_warning
}
```

## R

```{.webgeods-r #buffer-proximity-r}
#| package: sf, jsonlite
library(sf)

FALLBACK_NAMES <- c("shop", "road segment", "building")
fallback_geom <- st_sfc(
  st_point(c(12.4700, 41.9000)),
  st_linestring(rbind(c(12.4720, 41.9010), c(12.4740, 41.9005))),
  st_polygon(list(rbind(
    c(12.4678, 41.8988), c(12.4682, 41.8988),
    c(12.4682, 41.8992), c(12.4678, 41.8992), c(12.4678, 41.8988)
  ))),
  crs = 4326
)

data <- NULL
for (path in c("/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip")) {
  data <- tryCatch(st_read(path, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(data)) break
}

crs_warning <- NULL
if (is.null(data)) {
  data <- st_sf(name = FALLBACK_NAMES, geometry = fallback_geom)
} else if (is.na(st_crs(data))) {
  st_crs(data) <- 4326
  crs_warning <- "No CRS found in the uploaded file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
} else if (!isTRUE(st_crs(data) == st_crs(4326))) {
  data <- st_transform(data, 4326)
}
if (!("name" %in% names(data))) {
  data$name <- paste("feature", seq_len(nrow(data)))
}

# UTM auto-pick from the bounding-box center -- see section 1 above.
bnd <- st_bbox(data)
center_lon <- (bnd[["xmin"]] + bnd[["xmax"]]) / 2
center_lat <- (bnd[["ymin"]] + bnd[["ymax"]]) / 2
utm_zone <- floor((center_lon + 180) / 6) + 1
calc_epsg <- if (center_lat >= 0) 32600 + utm_zone else 32700 + utm_zone

data_proj <- st_transform(data, calc_epsg)
buffered <- st_buffer(data_proj, 30)

# A single UTM zone can map far-away features to infinity. sf
# tolerates it without erroring -- an inf-coordinate st_buffer() just
# comes back empty -- but an empty buffer is still a feature that
# silently produced nothing, so it's excluded here instead, with a
# clear count.
finite_mask <- !st_is_empty(buffered)
excluded_count <- as.integer(sum(!finite_mask))
if (!any(finite_mask)) {
  stop(paste0(
    "None of the ", nrow(data), " features could be projected into a ",
    "single UTM zone (EPSG:", calc_epsg, ") -- this dataset spans too wide ",
    "an area for this article's single-zone approach. Try a smaller, more ",
    "local file."
  ))
}
buffered <- buffered[finite_mask, ]

result <- list(
  calculationCrs = jsonlite::unbox(paste0("EPSG:", calc_epsg)),
  geometryTypes = as.character(st_geometry_type(data)),
  bufferGeometryTypes = as.character(st_geometry_type(buffered)),
  bufferAreas = round(as.numeric(st_area(buffered)), 1),
  excludedCount = jsonlite::unbox(excluded_count),
  crsWarning = if (is.null(crs_warning)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(crs_warning)
)
jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

## 4. One distance, three different shapes

The numbers below describe the built-in fallback specifically (a
point, a line, and a polygon, buffered 30m). If you uploaded your
own file instead, the areas will differ, but the same three rules
still explain whatever shape came out. Both cards above ran the exact
same 30m buffer on the exact same three features. The shapes agree
exactly; the areas don't, by a small, fully explainable margin, not
a disagreement about the answer:

- The **point's** buffer is a circle: every direction from a single
  location is equally "within reach."
- The **line's** buffer is a stadium shape (a rectangle with two
  rounded ends): every point along its length gets its own circle of
  reach, and they merge into one continuous zone.
- The **polygon's** buffer is the original shape, expanded outward,
  with its corners rounded off: everywhere already inside stays
  inside, plus a 30m halo all the way around the boundary.

::: {.callout-note}
**Why the point buffer's area isn't quite identical.** A circle can't
be drawn exactly with straight line segments: every buffer
implementation approximates it with a many-sided polygon, and *how*
closely depends on how many segments it uses per quarter-circle.
GeoPandas' `.buffer()` defaults to `resolution=16`; `sf::st_buffer()`
defaults to `nQuadSegs=30`, almost double. A true 30m-radius circle
has an area of 2827.4 m² (`π × 30²`). Python's 16-segment
approximation lands at 2822.9 m²; R's 30-segment one at 2826.1 m²,
closer to the true value, because it's a finer approximation of the
*same* circle, not a different formula. Passing `resolution=30` in
Python reproduces R's default result almost exactly (2826.1416 m²,
verified); the defaults just don't happen to agree out of the box.
:::

**Every geometry type buffers into a polygon**, regardless of what it
started as: there's no such thing as a "buffered point" that's still
a point. That's also why dissolving several overlapping buffers into
one shape (the standalone tool's own checkbox) is meaningful: once
everything is already a polygon, merging overlapping ones is a single,
well-defined operation, the same one used to answer "what's the total
area within reach of *any* of these features," not "within reach of
each one separately."
